extracted.intended_audience: Reuters journalists, reporters, photographers, editors and other news staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for ethical, accurate and legally safe newsgathering and sourcing: how to cultivate, deal with, attribute and verify sources; how to handle interviews, datelines, anonymous sources, rumours, competitors' pickups, social media, children, public figures and people stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific claims and epidemic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent confirmation or expert peer review is required for any story about a major scientific advance; avoid hype in coverage of epidemics and seek to quantify the statistical risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cope with loose talk about miracle cures and scientific breakthroughs; require independent confirmation or expert peer review before reporting major advances; seek to quantify statistical risk when covering epidemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining attention to crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: If what seems like a routine murder is getting extensive attention, explain why, quoting qualified commentators and beware groups with vested interests seeking to exploit or sensationalise crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that some crimes may legitimately become iconic by touching a public nerve; question motives of campaigns that sensationalise crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing children
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed with caution when interviewing children, especially trauma victims and child soldiers; only interview a child when the interview is crucial to telling an important story, taking utmost care to avoid exposing the minor to harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimise stress for the child; in normal circumstances obtain permission from an appropriate authority (parent, guardian, school); observe severe restrictions on talking to children involved in criminal proceedings and on identifying minors in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs private for figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between public and private spheres for people newsworthy because of their profession; ensure references to personal lives of politicians, royals or corporate executives are broadly relevant to their role, policies or chosen image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a public figure should not make every aspect of life fair game; public figures who bring families or personal attributes into the spotlight should expect scrutiny of those areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question sources' motives with powerful figures
rubrics_metrics.description: With coverage of rich, famous or powerful people, question sources' motives at every step and be on high alert for smears and self-promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat assertions about public figures critically and check for manipulation or promotional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment and celebrity sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment stories must meet rigorous standards; do not rush to pick up dubiously sourced stories about entertainers merely because they will get wide play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote media celebrities for topics they are qualified to speak on (acting, industry); have a good reason to quote showbiz stars on other matters (e.g., politics); be wary of tabloid-style typecasting and the fact that some public figures may decline the right to reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness in people stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether your own emotions (envy, distrust, empathy, pride) may skew your writing and obscure the story; imagine how subjects would react to the story before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subjects would love the story you may have been spun; if reaction is likely negative, ensure you can defend the approach as accurate and fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition vs ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition should not lead to ethical lapses such as plagiarism and fabrication; responsible journalists never sacrifice ethics in pursuit of a byline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain editorial and ethical standards even when pursuing scoops or competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuters sourcing principle: on-the-spot and named sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reuters journalist or camera is always the best source on a witnessed event; a named source is always preferable to an unnamed source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deliberate misleading in sourcing; do not quote a source as saying one thing on the record and the opposite on background; do not cite sources in the plural when you have only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivating sources: professional distance and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources must be cultivated professionally and politely while maintaining detachment; disclose romantic or family attachments with sources and avoid reporting on or quoting family members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay your own way when appropriate; avoid spending so much leisure time with a source that it raises perception of bias; if in doubt, seek managerial guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with sources: establish attribution terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with sources identify yourself, establish the basis of the conversation (on-the-record, off-the-record, background), and be familiar with local ground rules; negotiate clear attribution and stick to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear the circumstances (e.g., 'said in a statement', 'told reporters in answer to questions'); do not use passive sourcing like 'it was announced' or 'it was learned'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview technique and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use open-ended questions to start sources talking; closed questions to confirm facts; avoid multipart questions and ask one question at a time; verify identity and contact details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check telephone numbers and spelling; if in doubt about identity call back via company/organisation switchboard; resist requests to see quotes or submit stories for approval; if quotes must be approved, do not allow material change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and retaining information
rubrics_metrics.description: Record information from sources by taking notes, saving digital notes, or tape recording (with permission where required) and retain notes, tapes, video or other information for at least two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are encouraged to learn shorthand; if writing quotes directly to a screen save and print a copy; do not write the story directly from the screen to preserve evidence for legal defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to source statements
rubrics_metrics.description: You must source every statement in every story unless it is an established fact or clearly in the public domain or when the reporter/photographer/camera operator was on the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the source of a quote quickly (usually after the first sentence); do not run quotes from different speakers together; use transition sentences between speakers; if an event is not contentious you may lead without a source but sourcing must appear high in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of sourcing within a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to source every story within the first two paragraphs; the more important the story, the sooner it must be sourced — great import stories should be sourced in the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contentious statements must be sourced each time they appear; alerts and newsbreaks require sourcing unless clearly official or scheduled; special rules apply when source is major figure or the source is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradation and hierarchy of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reuters journalist or camera on the spot is the best source; first-hand reports deal with facts, not opinions; when Reuters is the witness source as 'REUTERS WITNESS'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the witness saw unexpected or contentious elements, describe them specifically (e.g., 'Reuters photographer John Smith saw police...'). For routine scheduled public events witnessing may not require sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for named sources and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible identify sources by name and position; specificity enables readers to gauge accuracy and protects the story if challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even named sources should be checked and balanced in conflict situations; negotiate to identify sources who initially refuse to be named; avoid using anonymous sources when named sources are readily available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and ranking of anonymous/unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnamed sources must have direct knowledge or represent an authority with direct knowledge; reliability declines the further removed the source is from the event; negotiate precise descriptions of anonymous sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories based on anonymous sources should normally have two or three sources; do not use vague descriptions like 'a source' or 'sources' without further detail; unnamed sources rank: authoritative (exercises real authority), official (company spokesman), designated (diplomatic, conference, intelligence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-source story approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories based on a single, anonymous source should be exceptional and require approval by an immediate supervisor who must be satisfied the source is authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisor should consider the source's track record and the reporter's track record; approval should be noted on outgoing copy in the 'edited by' sign-off; supervisors may pre-delegate approval to experienced senior correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policing sourcing and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are expected to disclose their sources to their immediate supervisor when asked; protection of confidentiality is paramount and names should not be put in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors should only enquire for legitimate editorial reasons; they should not disclose names when discussing concerns (discuss nature/position/access instead); desk editors may not ask a reporter to identify a source by name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in sourcing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Be honest and never deliberately mislead the reader; never use pseudonyms, never cite plural when only one source; in disputes try to speak to all sides and make clear which side your source is on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not quote the same source both on-the-record and off-the-record in contradictory ways; it is permissible to omit an on-the-record comment if the source has given off-the-record material, but if on-the-record comment is needed seek another individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline accuracy and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dateline only if staff (text, pictures or TV) are on the spot and are providing information; for news datelines can be used up to 24 hours after leaving the scene (with caveats); for features an off-base dateline may be kept up to a month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a dateline before having staff on the spot; run stories without datelines only in exceptional cases authorised by a specialist editor and bureau chief for safety or access reasons; items that are tabular or established background facts do not take datelines; signoff should identify where the story was written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding manipulation and weighing motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Every source has a motive — identify it and weigh the 'spin' against other information, known background and common sense; talk to sources on all sides and seek at least one source from each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greatest weight to sources with proven accuracy; be wary even of trusted sources (e.g., banker's bonus may bias them); listen for what is NOT said; play devil's advocate and try to disprove as well as prove; seek independent third parties for perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and right to reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Always give people, companies or organisations the chance to answer any charges levelled against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with guidelines on legal dangers and attention editor items and hoaxes; seek to present answers from those accused when practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking back with sources vs vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit stories, scripts or images to sources for vetting before publication; you may check back to verify a quote or factual information but must avoid giving sources opportunity to retract or materially alter quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist requests to see quotes; if no option, give a tight deadline and do not agree to material changes; allow linguistic clean-up for non-native speakers but do not change meaning; if a source asks to change substantial information, drop the quote or do not run the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling allegations and vituperative anonymous attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow sources to make allegations, contentious statements or vituperative attacks behind a cloak of anonymity; use unnamed sources for facts, not opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require on-the-record attribution for vituperative attacks; may waive only if a senior official makes a considered policy statement that is obviously newsworthy; otherwise refuse the story if anonymous source insists on vituperative attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting rumours
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters aims to report facts, not rumours; when rumour affects markets follow strict procedures to verify or report carefully without spreading unconfirmed claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure from at least two sources what the rumour is; attempt to determine whether it is true; write a report saying spokespeople unavailable if necessary; in exceptional fast-moving markets have a second reporter check while story is written, keep description vague, state you are checking urgently; follow up with confirmatory or denial items and avoid repeating unconfirmed rumours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickups from competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: When picking up reports from other media, name the source (newspaper, website, broadcaster or news agency) and make every effort to check a pickup rather than simply rely on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another organisation's report is moving markets, immediately issue a story explaining why, only after you have seen/heard/read the report yourself; make clear the report has not been confirmed and that Reuters is checking it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using vague 'reports' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'reports' or 'unconfirmed reports' as the basis for a story; avoid using 'reported' as an unspecific source in headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forced by space, specify the source in the lead; avoid phrases like 'it was not known' — use a source (e.g., 'Police said they did not know…').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing Reuters products
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting figures from Reuters products, clearly source the information to 'Reuters data'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not necessary for real-time prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of analysts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not quote vaguely 'analysts'; specify their area of expertise (e.g., 'a strategic affairs analyst with the U.S. Council on Foreign Relations in New York').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic 'analysts' which convey little about reliability or proximity to the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of the obvious need not be sourced
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need to source statements of the obvious (e.g., 'Destruction of half its army is a serious blow to Rome, military analysts said.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment about what counts as 'obvious' background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media is a tip; verification required
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter and similar sites are virtual venues where users may post useful material, but they are not sources per se; material from such sites often serves as a tip that must be checked and verified before use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'source' a story to Twitter as you would to a press conference; use strict verification criteria for textual, video or photographic material; be wary of 'sleeper' or 'shadow' accounts designed to peddle misinformation; checks include basic Google searches and cross-referencing with reputable sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and transparency for social media material
rubrics_metrics.description: When using official information from Twitter mention that the information comes from Twitter and, when using material from users, refer in text to 'Twitter users said/posted xxx' and say how much is known about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about provenance and whether you were able to contact the poster directly; provide hyperlinks to Twitter pages where possible; limit statements about veracity if you cannot confirm the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making and approval for using social media material
rubrics_metrics.description: Text and visuals editors at HQ and journalists in the field must coordinate and only senior editors may approve running material from social sites; consult in-house counsel where possible before running images or information from social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider safety of journalists and risk of reprisals; each decision to use material is a calculated risk balancing newsworthiness against reputational harm; only senior editors may decide if news value trumps need to get permission from copyright holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and restrictions for social media visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Any image that is at all suspicious should be spiked; try to find the source of visuals and verify date and location; limit use to minimum essential images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If origin cannot be verified, restrict use to essential iconic images; be mindful of copyright—seek permission from originator where possible; avoid using images of commercial origin without permission unless senior editor authorises use on news-value grounds.
